q: Answer these questions about libraries.
parts: Which Scottish-American steel magnate paid for more than 2,500 public libraries?
The Library of Congress is located in which city?
Which clergyman's bequest of books in 1638 helped found a college in Massachusetts that now bears his name?

q: This poet-philosopher from Colophon wrote that Ethiopians make their gods snub-nosed and black, while Thracians make theirs blue-eyed and red-haired. He added that if horses or oxen had hands, they would draw gods in their own likeness. He argued for a single god unlike mortals in body or thought. For 10 points, name this pre-Socratic critic of anthropomorphic religion.

This student of Parmenides devised arguments against plurality and motion, including one in which a swift runner can never overtake a slow tortoise with a head start. Another says that an arrow in flight is always at rest at each instant. Plato depicts him in a dialogue with the elderly Parmenides. For 10 points, name this Eleatic philosopher of paradoxes.

This Milesian thought that air is the basic stuff of the cosmos and that other substances arise from it by rarefaction and condensation. He was a student of Anaximander and reasoned that the soul is air, like the breath. Aristotle called air his first principle. For 10 points, name this pre-Socratic whose name ends in "-menes."

The Great World-System is attributed to this thinker, the earliest known atomist, whose existence was doubted by Epicurus. He argued that void exists, contradicting Parmenides, because motion requires empty space. His pupil Democritus developed his teachings. For 10 points, name this pre-Socratic whose name suggests "white horse."

In his work On Non-Being, this sophist argued that nothing exists, that even if something did, it could not be known, and that if known, it could not be communicated. He also composed a speech defending Helen of Troy. A Platonic dialogue is named for him. For 10 points, name this rhetorician from Leontini.

This Athenian, a pupil of Socrates, taught at the Cynosarges gymnasium and is traditionally called the founder of Cynicism. He held that virtue is sufficient for happiness and that "virtue is a matter of deeds, not words." He wrote works including a lost treatise on Odysseus and Ajax. For 10 points, name this teacher of Diogenes.

This pupil of Socrates from Cyrene founded a school that held that immediate bodily pleasure is the goal of life. He accepted payment for teaching and lived luxuriously at the court of Dionysius of Syracuse. He reportedly said, "I possess, but am not possessed." For 10 points, name this founder of the Cyrenaics.

This third head of the Stoic school developed a form of propositional logic with connectives such as "if" and "or." He is said to have written over seven hundred works, none of which survive intact. He argued that fate and responsibility are compatible by using the analogy of a cylinder rolling down a slope. For 10 points, name this Stoic from Soli.

The Outlines of Pyrrhonism and Against the Mathematicians are by this physician and skeptic of the second century AD. His works are the main surviving source for ancient skepticism, including the Ten Modes of Aenesidemus. He argued that suspension of judgment leads to tranquility. For 10 points, name this author of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism.

This Tyrian pupil of Plotinus edited and published his master's lectures and wrote a biography of him. His Introduction to Aristotle's Categories posed a question about whether genera and species exist in reality or only in the mind, a problem that dominated medieval logic. He also wrote Against the Christians. For 10 points, name this Neoplatonist whose Tree is a classification chart.

Imprisoned in Pavia and awaiting execution for treason under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, this former consul wrote a dialogue with Lady Philosophy. He translated much of Aristotle's logical works into Latin and wrote the Consolation of Philosophy. He also wrote on music and arithmetic. For 10 points, name this Roman statesman and philosopher.

This Jewish thinker from Egypt applied allegorical readings to the Torah and described the Logos as an intermediary between God and creation. He led a delegation of Alexandrian Jews to the emperor Caligula. He wrote On the Creation of the World and Allegorical Interpretation. For 10 points, name this first-century philosopher who blended Platonism with Judaism.

This Roman poet's hexameter work in six books explains the physics of Epicurus, including a "swerve" of atoms called the clinamen. It argues that fear of death is irrational and ends with a description of a plague in Athens. A manuscript was rediscovered by Poggio Bracciolini in 1417. For 10 points, name this author of De rerum natura.

This Roman consul exposed the conspiracy of Catiline in 63 BC and was later killed on the orders of Mark Antony. He introduced Greek philosophy to Latin readers in works such as On Duties and Tusculan Disputations. He was an Academic skeptic who wrote On the Nature of the Gods. For 10 points, name this Roman orator.

This head of the Academy visited Rome in 155 BC as part of an embassy and gave speeches arguing for justice one day and against it the next. Cato the Elder was alarmed and had the philosophers sent home. He developed a theory of probability as a guide to action while rejecting certain knowledge. For 10 points, name this skeptic from Cyrene.

This pupil of Aristotle succeeded him as head of the Lyceum and inherited his library. Born on Lesbos, he wrote the Characters, which sketches thirty types of unpleasant people, and an Enquiry into Plants. His name, given by Aristotle, means "divine speaker." For 10 points, name this founder of botany.

This Confucian argued that human nature is bad and that people become good only through education and ritual. He taught Han Feizi and Li Si. His book, named for him, includes a chapter "Encouraging Learning" and another on Heaven, which he said does not act for human purposes. For 10 points, name this pessimistic rival of Mencius.

This Chinese thinker's school argued for jian ai, or "impartial care," holding that everyone should be loved equally. He condemned offensive war, expensive funerals, and ritual music as wasteful. His followers, the Mohists, formed a disciplined brotherhood. For 10 points, name this rival of Confucius.

This Chinese Legalist, a student of Xunzi, argued that a ruler should combine fa, or law, shu, or technique, and shi, or positional power. The King of Qin admired his writings, but he died in prison after being slandered by Li Si. His work includes parables such as the man who waited by a stump for another rabbit. For 10 points, name this author of a book that bears his name.

In this dialogue, Socrates compares himself to a midwife who helps deliver ideas. The title character, a young mathematician, offers three definitions of knowledge: perception, true judgment, and true judgment with an account. The dialogue ends without a definition. For 10 points, name this Platonic dialogue on the nature of knowledge.

This last and longest dialogue of Plato, with twelve books, has an Athenian Stranger converse with Cleinias and Megillus about regulations for a colony on Crete. It proposes a Nocturnal Council and a second-best city to the ideal one. It lacks Socrates as a character. For 10 points, name this work.

In this work, Aristotle opens by saying that "all men by nature desire to know." He studies "being qua being" and criticizes the Forms in Book Alpha. Book Lambda discusses the unmoved mover and eternal substance. For 10 points, name this work, which he called "first philosophy."

This treatise by Aristotle defines the soul as the form of a living body and distinguishes the nutritive, perceptive, and rational capacities. Its third book describes an active intellect that makes all things. It also discusses the five senses and the common sense. For 10 points, name this work whose Latin title is De Anima.

This treatise by Aristotle lists ten kinds of predicate: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and affection. It distinguishes primary substances, such as an individual man, from secondary substances. It is the first work in his collection on logic. For 10 points, name this treatise.

This work introduces mimesis as the basis of art and says that a tragedy must have plot, character, thought, diction, melody, and spectacle. It introduces the ideas of hamartia, anagnorisis, and catharsis. A planned second book on comedy is lost. For 10 points, name this treatise by Aristotle on drama.

This work by Aristotle says that humans are by nature political animals. It classifies governments as monarchy, aristocracy, and polity, with corresponding bad forms tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy. It praises a large middle class as the basis of a stable state. For 10 points, name this treatise on government.

Plato gave the first version of this argument in his Parmenides, and Aristotle named it in his critique. It argues that if a man is a man by resembling the Form of Man, a further Form is required to explain the resemblance, and so on infinitely. It is a regress argument against a metaphysical theory. For 10 points, name this argument that threatens the Theory of Forms, named after a number.

This Syrian pupil of Porphyry defended theurgy, ritual practices that unite the soul with the gods, in On the Mysteries of the Egyptians. He wrote a Life of Pythagoras and organized a curriculum of Platonic dialogues. He founded a school in Apamea. For 10 points, name this Neoplatonist from Chalcis.

This fifth-century Neoplatonist was a leading head of the Academy in Athens. His Elements of Theology lists 211 propositions on the One, the many, and a hierarchy of levels of reality. He wrote a commentary on the first book of Euclid's Elements. For 10 points, name this successor of Syrianus, born in Constantinople.

In this dialogue, Hermogenes asks whether names are correct by nature or by convention. The title character, a follower of Heraclitus, says that names are natural, and Socrates offers many playful etymologies. It is Plato's main work on language. For 10 points, name this dialogue named after a Heraclitean.
Answer these questions about Aristotle's ethics.
parts: What Greek term for "practical wisdom" lets a person judge the right action in particular situations?
What Greek term for "weakness of will" names acting against one's better judgment?
What Greek term for a settled disposition or habit, acquired by repeated practice, underlies Aristotle's account of virtue?

q: Answer these questions about the Cynics.
parts: Which Cynic from Sinope reportedly lived in a large jar?
Which Cynic from Thebes gave away his wealth and was the teacher of Zeno of Citium?
Which woman from Maroneia gave up her wealth to marry a Cynic from Thebes and live as a Cynic herself?

q: Answer these questions about Aristotle's four causes.
parts: Which cause is the matter out of which something is made, such as the bronze of a statue?
Which cause is the purpose or end for which a thing exists?
Which cause is the source of change, such as the sculptor who makes a statue?

q: Answer these questions about early Chinese texts.
parts: Which ancient Chinese divination text, whose name means "Book of Changes," is built from sixty-four figures?
What name is given to the figures made of six stacked broken or unbroken lines?
Which of the Four Books, traditionally attributed to Confucius's grandson Zisi, advocates balance?

q: Answer these questions about the death of Socrates in Plato's dialogues.
parts: In which dialogue does Socrates, in prison, refuse to escape when urged by a friend?
In that dialogue, which personified entities does Socrates imagine arguing that he must obey them?
His execution was delayed by a religious mission to which island, where a ship was sent each year?

q: Answer these questions about Plato's Phaedrus.
parts: In Phaedrus, Socrates compares the soul to a charioteer with how many winged horses?
Which Egyptian god does Socrates say invented writing, which the king Thamus criticized?
Phaedrus reads aloud a speech on love by which orator?

q: Answer these questions about Plato in Sicily.
parts: Plato visited which Sicilian city to advise its tyrants?
Which tyrant of the city hosted Aristippus and later Plato, and was succeeded by his son?
Which student of Plato and kinsman of the tyrants tried to reform the city?

q: Answer these questions about Stoic terms.
parts: What Greek term for "breath" names the Stoic material that pervades the cosmos?
What Greek term for freedom from passions was an ideal of the Stoic sage?
What term names the periodic destruction of the cosmos by fire in Stoic cosmology?

q: This Moravian-born student of Franz Brentano wrote Logical Investigations and Ideas. His late, unfinished work warned of a crisis in European sciences caused by forgetting the "life-world." He urged philosophers to return "to the things themselves." Martin Heidegger dedicated a major work to him. For 10 points, name this founder of phenomenology.

This philosopher served as rector of the University of Freiburg in 1933 and joined the Nazi party. Later essays such as "The Question Concerning Technology" discuss "enframing" and the "Letter on Humanism." He had an affair with his student Hannah Arendt and lived in a hut at Todtnauberg. For 10 points, name this German philosopher of being.

This Jena professor developed a formal logic with quantifiers in his 1879 Begriffsschrift. He defended logicism in The Foundations of Arithmetic. Bertrand Russell's 1902 letter showing a paradox in his Basic Laws of Arithmetic crushed him. He distinguished between sense and reference. For 10 points, name this German logician.

This philosopher's The Logical Structure of the World attempted to reduce all knowledge to elementary experience. His essay "The Elimination of Metaphysics through Logical Analysis of Language" mocked Heidegger's remarks about "the Nothing." His "principle of tolerance" lets one choose among different linguistic frameworks. For 10 points, name this Vienna Circle member who moved to Chicago.

This American logician argued in "Two Dogmas of Empiricism" against the analytic-synthetic distinction. In Word and Object, he argued for the indeterminacy of translation using the example of a native speaker who says "gavagai." He said "to be is to be the value of a bound variable." For 10 points, name this Harvard philosopher.

This Viennese-born philosopher wrote The Logic of Scientific Discovery and The Open Society and Its Enemies. He argued that scientific theories can never be proven but only falsified. He criticized the claims of Freudian psychoanalysis and astrology as unfalsifiable. For 10 points, name this author of Conjectures and Refutations.

This author argued that science proceeds through long periods of "normal science" punctuated by crises and revolutions. He used the term "paradigm shift" and wrote The Copernican Revolution. His 1962 book argues that rival paradigms may be incommensurable. For 10 points, name this author of The Structure of Scientific Revolutions.

This philosopher's 1974 essay asks whether we can know what it is like to be a creature that uses echolocation, arguing that subjective experience cannot be captured by physical description. He also wrote The View from Nowhere and Mortal Questions. He taught at New York University. For 10 points, name this author of "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?"

This political theorist's book The Origins of Totalitarianism appeared in 1951. She covered Adolf Eichmann's trial in Jerusalem and wrote about the "banality of evil." In The Human Condition, she distinguishes labor, work, and action. For 10 points, name this German-born philosopher, a student of Heidegger and Jaspers.

This French thinker's Discipline and Punish uses Bentham's Panopticon as a model of modern surveillance. His multivolume History of Sexuality argues that sexuality is produced by discourse and power. He held a chair at the College de France and wrote The Order of Things. For 10 points, name this theorist of "biopower."

This philosopher's Speech and Phenomena criticizes Husserl, and Of Grammatology critiques the privileging of speech over writing, which he called "logocentrism." He coined the word "differance," spelled with an "a." He is associated with deconstruction. For 10 points, name this Algerian-born French thinker.

This French phenomenologist wrote Phenomenology of Perception, which stresses the role of the lived body as the ground of experience. He co-founded the journal Les Temps modernes with Jean-Paul Sartre but later broke with him. His unfinished final work was The Visible and the Invisible. For 10 points, name this author who developed the notion of "flesh."

This student of Heidegger wrote Truth and Method, which defended the role of tradition and prejudice in interpretation. He introduced the "fusion of horizons" as a model for understanding. He taught at Heidelberg and debated Jurgen Habermas. For 10 points, name this German philosopher of hermeneutics.

This German philosopher wrote The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere and The Theory of Communicative Action. He proposed discourse ethics, in which norms are valid if all affected could accept them in rational discussion. He is the leading figure of the second generation of the Frankfurt School. For 10 points, name this thinker.

This member of the Frankfurt School wrote Minima Moralia and Negative Dialectics. He wrote that "to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric" and criticized the "culture industry." He studied the roots of authoritarianism in the 1950 study The Authoritarian Personality. For 10 points, name this author of Aesthetic Theory.

This American wrote The Varieties of Religious Experience and a pioneering textbook, The Principles of Psychology. He popularized the term "stream of consciousness" and defended the "will to believe." His brother was the novelist Henry. For 10 points, name this Harvard pragmatist.

This logician and founder of pragmatism wrote "How to Make Our Ideas Clear." He distinguished icons, indices, and symbols in a theory of signs called semiotics. He also introduced abduction as a form of inference. He worked for the United States Coast Survey. For 10 points, name this American thinker.

This Vermont-born philosopher founded the Laboratory School at the University of Chicago and wrote Democracy and Education. In Art as Experience, he held that art arises from the ordinary processes of living. He championed instrumentalism, in which ideas are tools for solving problems. For 10 points, name this progressive pragmatist.

This Cambridge philosopher's Principia Ethica argued that "good" is a simple, indefinable property. He called attempts to define it in natural terms the "naturalistic fallacy" and posed the "open question" argument. In "Proof of an External World," he held up his hands as evidence. For 10 points, name this British analytic philosopher.

In Language, Truth and Logic, this British philosopher defended the verification principle, which says that a statement is meaningful only if it is analytic or empirically verifiable. He visited Vienna as a young man and brought logical positivism to Britain. He taught at Oxford. For 10 points, name this author of The Problem of Knowledge.

This Oxford philosopher's William James Lectures, published as How to Do Things with Words, distinguished constative from performative utterances. He divided speech acts into locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts. His Sense and Sensibilia criticizes sense-datum theory. For 10 points, name this ordinary language philosopher.

This philosopher's lectures at Princeton, published as Naming and Necessity, argued that proper names are rigid designators. He argued that some necessary truths are knowable only a posteriori, such as that water is H2O. He also gave a skeptical reading of Wittgenstein on rule-following. For 10 points, name this author who developed possible-world semantics for modal logic.

This Oxford philosopher's Reasons and Persons discusses a teletransporter that destroys and recreates a person on Mars. He argued that personal identity is not what matters, and he posed the Repugnant Conclusion about population ethics. He also wrote On What Matters. For 10 points, name this author of a book that uses the non-identity problem.

This translator of Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations coined the term "consequentialism" in her 1958 essay "Modern Moral Philosophy." Her book Intention analyzed practical reasoning. She opposed awarding an honorary degree to Harry Truman. For 10 points, name this Catholic philosopher who helped revive virtue ethics.

This French Oratorian priest wrote The Search After Truth. He held that God is the only true cause and that created things are mere occasions, a doctrine called occasionalism. He argued that we see all things in God. For 10 points, name this Cartesian whose Dialogues on Metaphysics were widely read.

This Scottish philosopher wrote An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense. He criticized the "way of ideas" of Locke, Berkeley, and Hume as leading to skepticism. He taught at Glasgow and defended direct realism about perception. For 10 points, name this founder of the Scottish school of common sense.

This Irish-born philosopher at Glasgow developed a theory that people possess a "moral sense." His An Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue used the phrase "the greatest happiness for the greatest numbers." He taught Adam Smith. For 10 points, name this Scottish Enlightenment thinker.

This French philosopher's Creative Evolution describes an "elan vital" that drives life. In Time and Free Will, he distinguished the lived time of duration from clock time. He won the 1927 Nobel Prize in Literature. For 10 points, name this author of Matter and Memory who debated Albert Einstein on time.

This student of Kant wrote the Wissenschaftslehre, a system in which the I posits itself and the Not-I. He was dismissed from Jena in 1799 after the atheism controversy. His Addresses to the German Nation urged a national education against Napoleonic domination. For 10 points, name this German idealist.

This German thinker argued in The Essence of Christianity that God is a projection of human qualities. He was a Young Hegelian who turned against his teacher's idealism. Karl Marx wrote eleven theses about him. For 10 points, name this author who wrote that "man is what he eats."
Answer these questions about Heidegger's concepts.
parts: Which 1927 book by Heidegger analyzes human existence in terms of care, anxiety, and being-toward-death?
What German term, literally "being there," names the human kind of being analyzed in that book?
What term, from the German Geworfenheit, names the fact that we find ourselves already placed in a world not of our choosing?

q: Answer these questions about phenomenology.
parts: Husserl's method sets aside assumptions about the existence of the external world through what Greek-named procedure, also called bracketing?
What term, central to Brentano and Husserl, describes the directedness of mental states toward objects?
Which Heidegger-influenced Lithuanian-born French philosopher wrote Totality and Infinity, centering on ethics and the face of the Other?

q: Answer these questions about a Marxist-influenced circle of German thinkers.
parts: Adorno, Marcuse, and Horkheimer were members of a Marxist-influenced circle named for which German city?
Adorno and Horkheimer co-wrote which 1947 book on the self-destructive tendency of reason?
Which member of this group wrote One-Dimensional Man and Eros and Civilization?

q: Answer these questions about structuralism.
parts: Which Swiss linguist's Course in General Linguistics distinguished the signifier from the signified?
Which anthropologist wrote Tristes Tropiques and The Savage Mind?
Which critic's 1967 essay declared "The Death of the Author"?

q: Answer these questions about philosophy of mind in the Oxford school.
parts: Which Oxford philosopher wrote The Concept of Mind?
What phrase did Ryle use for Cartesian dualism, which he mocked as a "ghost" in a "machine"?
What type of error did Ryle say was committed by treating the mind as a thing of the same logical type as the body?

q: Answer these questions about a twentieth-century liberal thinker.
parts: Which philosopher, born in Riga, gave the lecture "Two Concepts of Liberty"?
What term names the kind of freedom this thinker described as the absence of interference by others?
This thinker's essay "The Hedgehog and the Fox" is about which Russian novelist?

q: Answer these questions about metaethics.
parts: Which "boo-hurrah" theory holds that moral statements express emotions rather than facts?
Which view, defended by J. L. Mackie, holds that moral claims purport to describe objective facts but are all false?
Which view, associated with R. M. Hare, holds that moral judgments are universalizable commands?

q: Answer these questions about Jewish and religious thinkers of the twentieth century.
parts: Which Austrian-born philosopher wrote I and Thou, contrasting two kinds of relation?
Which German psychiatrist-turned-philosopher coined the term "Axial Age"?
Which German Jewish philosopher, a friend of Buber, wrote The Star of Redemption?

q: A famous 1963 three-page paper uses characters named Smith and Jones, with one of them having ten coins in his pocket, to present counterexamples. It shows that a belief can be true and justified but still not count as knowledge because the justification is connected to the truth only by luck. The paper was published in Analysis by a professor then at Wayne State University. For 10 points, name this problem in epistemology, which attacks the traditional definition of knowledge.

This Franciscan friar from a village in Surrey was summoned to Avignon in 1324 and fled to the court of Louis of Bavaria in Munich. He wrote the Summa Logicae and defended the view that universals are only names, not real things. He also argued against the pope in the poverty controversy. For 10 points, name this English scholastic philosopher.

This Dominican friar was burned at the stake in the Campo de' Fiori in Rome in 1600. He taught that the universe is infinite and contains innumerable worlds, and defended Copernicus's heliocentric system. He was denounced to the Venetian Inquisition by Giovanni Mocenigo. For 10 points, name this Italian philosopher and former friar who wrote about the art of memory.

This French logician and theologian wrote Sic et Non, a collection of contradictory statements by church fathers. His autobiography, the Historia Calamitatum, tells of his love for a student and his castration by hired thugs. He taught at Paris and debated William of Champeaux on universals. For 10 points, name this lover of Heloise.

In 1802, William Paley published a book arguing that if one found a pocket watch on a heath, one would infer a watchmaker, and so complex living things imply a designer. Charles Darwin later offered a naturalistic alternative. Hume had criticized an earlier version in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion. For 10 points, name this style of argument for God from the order of the world, also called teleological.

This position holds that free will and determinism can both be true, because freedom means acting according to one's own desires without external constraint. Hume and the 1969 paper by Harry Frankfurt on alternate possibilities are important sources. It is sometimes called "soft determinism." For 10 points, name this view that rejects the idea that determinism rules out free will.

This view holds that mind or experience is a fundamental feature of all matter, rather than something that emerges only in brains. Spinoza and Alfred North Whitehead are cited as precursors, and Galen Strawson and Philip Goff defend modern versions. It faces a "combination problem" about how small minds form larger ones. For 10 points, name this theory of consciousness whose name means "all mind."

This Persian thinker, whose crisis of faith around 1095 led him to leave a teaching post at the Nizamiyya in Baghdad, attacked the Aristotelians in The Incoherence of the Philosophers. His Revival of the Religious Sciences defends Sufism within Sunni orthodoxy. He argued that causes are not necessary connections. For 10 points, name this Muslim theologian whose critic was Averroes.

This thirteenth-century Japanese monk traveled to China, where he studied under Rujing, and founded the Soto school of Zen in Japan. His massive work Shobogenzo calls for shikantaza, or "just sitting." He founded the monastery of Eihei-ji. For 10 points, name this Zen master who wrote on "being-time."

This eighth-century Indian philosopher wrote commentaries on the Brahma Sutras and the Upanishads, defending a nondualist reading in which only an undifferentiated reality is truly real. He taught that the world of appearances is maya, a kind of illusion. He founded monastic centers across India. For 10 points, name this founder of Advaita Vedanta.

In this thought experiment of William Newcomb, popularized by Robert Nozick, a being who is almost always right predicts whether you will take one box or two. The opaque box contains a million dollars if the being predicted you would take only it, and the other box always holds one thousand. Causal and evidential decision theory give different advice. For 10 points, name this paradox in decision theory.

Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice and Nel Noddings's Caring are the key texts for this approach, which holds that moral thinking should be centered on relationships and responsibilities rather than abstract rules. It arose as a critique of Lawrence Kohlberg's stages of moral development. Feminist thinkers developed it in the 1980s. For 10 points, name this approach in ethics.

This debate asks whether properties such as redness and triangularity exist independently of particular things. Realists such as Plato say they do, while nominalists deny it. Boethius translated a question about it from Porphyry, which began a medieval argument. For 10 points, name this classical metaphysical problem about general terms.

Carl Hempel posed this puzzle about confirmation: the statement "all ravens are black" is logically equivalent to "all non-black things are non-ravens." So seeing a white shoe seems to confirm that all ravens are black. For 10 points, name this paradox, also named for a black bird.

This argument for God's existence holds that whatever begins to exist has a cause, that the universe began to exist, and so the universe has a cause. It was developed by medieval Islamic theologians and revived by William Lane Craig. Its name comes from an Arabic word for speech or theology. For 10 points, name this cosmological argument.

Paul and Patricia Churchland defend this view, which holds that common-sense concepts of mind, such as belief and desire, form a false theory and will be replaced by neuroscience. It calls the common-sense framework "folk psychology." It is a radical form of physicalism. For 10 points, name this view that ordinary mental states do not exist.

This Italian wrote a Latin Oration that begins with the idea that human beings have no fixed nature and may shape themselves. At age twenty-three, he proposed nine hundred theses for public debate in Rome in 1486. The Church condemned some of his theses. For 10 points, name this Florentine author of the Oration on the Dignity of Man.

This Indian theologian, who headed a monastery at Srirangam, argued for "qualified nondualism," in which souls and the world are real parts of a personal God. He criticized the nondualism of Shankara and wrote a commentary on the Brahma Sutras called the Sri Bhashya. For 10 points, name this founder of Vishishtadvaita.

This Franciscan from Scotland, called the Subtle Doctor, argued that individuality comes from "haecceity," or thisness. He held that being is univocal when applied to God and creatures and emphasized the primacy of the will. Fidelity to the Immaculate Conception is associated with him. For 10 points, name this scholastic whose name gives us the word "dunce."

This Dominican mystic from Thuringia taught that the soul has a "spark" in which God is born, and he distinguished God from the "Godhead." He preached in German and was accused of heresy at Cologne and Avignon. Pope John XXII condemned some of his propositions in 1329 after his death. For 10 points, name this Rhineland mystic.

This cardinal from Kues wrote De docta ignorantia, or On Learned Ignorance, which says that human knowledge of God can only be conjecture. He taught the "coincidence of opposites" in the infinite and described the universe as having no fixed center. For 10 points, name this fifteenth-century German philosopher.

This principle in ethics says that causing a harm is permissible if the harm is a foreseen but unintended side effect and the act has a good aim. Thomas Aquinas's discussion of self-defense in the Summa is its traditional source. It is used to justify terminal sedation and some bombing. For 10 points, name this doctrine contrasting intending and foreseeing.

In a letter to Locke, William Molyneux asked whether a man born blind who learned to distinguish a cube from a sphere by touch would recognize them by sight when he first gained vision. Locke, Berkeley, and Leibniz discussed it. It bears on whether ideas of space are innate. For 10 points, name this problem named for an Irish scientist.

Nelson Goodman introduced this "new riddle of induction" in Fact, Fiction, and Forecast. Consider a predicate that applies to emeralds examined before a future time if they are green, and to others if they are blue. Evidence seems to support both generalizations equally. For 10 points, name this paradox whose predicate has a name similar to "green" and "blue."

This trilemma, named after a baron famed for pulling himself out of a swamp by his hair, says that any attempt to justify a belief ends in an infinite regress, a circle, or an arbitrary stopping point. Hans Albert popularized it. It is related to the skeptical Modes of Agrippa. For 10 points, name this problem in epistemology named for a German nobleman.

Donald Davidson used this relation to define a nonreductive form of materialism: there can be no difference in mental properties without a difference in physical properties. The idea says that mental properties depend on physical ones without being identical to them. Jaegwon Kim analyzed it extensively. For 10 points, name this relation of dependence in philosophy of mind and ethics.

This twelfth-century Neo-Confucian of the Song dynasty selected the Four Books as the core of Confucian education. He taught that all things are composed of li, or principle, and qi, or material force. His method of "investigation of things" influenced East Asian thought for centuries. For 10 points, name this scholar whose commentaries became the basis of civil service examinations.

This Ming dynasty Neo-Confucian is said to have achieved enlightenment while in exile at Longchang. He taught the unity of knowledge and action and held that "innate knowing," or liangzhi, is within the mind. His School of Mind opposed Zhu Xi's view. For 10 points, name this Chinese thinker.

This Japanese philosopher founded the Kyoto School and wrote An Inquiry into the Good, which develops the idea of "pure experience." He later developed a "logic of place." He walked daily along a canal path that now bears his name. For 10 points, name this philosopher who combined Zen with Western thought.

This Scottish-born philosopher's After Virtue argues that the Enlightenment project of justifying morality failed, leaving only fragments of earlier traditions. He called for a return to Aristotelian virtues, understood within practices and narrative unity of a life. He wrote A Short History of Ethics. For 10 points, name this author who contrasted Nietzsche with Aristotle.
Answer these questions about schools of Indian philosophy.
parts: Which school, attributed to Patanjali, teaches disciplined meditation and control of the mind?
Which school developed methods of logic and epistemology, including inference as a source of knowledge?
Which dualistic school distinguishes purusha, or consciousness, from prakriti, or matter?

q: Answer these questions about Jain and materialist thought in India.
parts: Which twenty-fourth teacher of Jainism, a contemporary of the Buddha, is credited with its present form?
What Jain doctrine holds that reality has many sides and that no single view captures the whole truth?
Which Indian school denied any afterlife and taught that only perception is reliable?

q: Answer these questions about Ibn Khaldun.
parts: Ibn Khaldun, who studied the rise and fall of dynasties, was born in which present-day Tunisian capital?
What is the title of his introduction to universal history, which treats history as a science?
What Arabic term for "group solidarity" does he say gives dynasties their power at first?

q: Answer these questions about theories of right action.
parts: Which theory holds that an act is right because God commands it?
Which view, developed by T. M. Scanlon, says that actions are wrong if they violate principles that no one could reasonably reject?
W. D. Ross called obligations such as keeping promises and gratitude what kind of duties, which can be overridden?

q: Answer these questions about theories of justification.
parts: Which theory holds that some beliefs are basic and support all other beliefs?
Which theory holds that a belief is justified when it fits within a mutually supporting web of beliefs?
Which theory, associated with Alvin Goldman, holds that a belief is justified if produced by a dependable process?

q: Answer these questions about views of God.
parts: What view holds that God created the world but does not intervene in it, as many Enlightenment thinkers believed?
What view identifies God with the universe as a whole?
What view holds that faith does not require or depend on reason?

q: Answer these questions about the foundations of logic.
parts: Which English mathematician wrote The Laws of Thought and gave his name to an algebra of true and false?
What pair of rules says that the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of negations?
Which logician proved the incompleteness theorems in 1931?

q: Answer these questions about the ethics of war.
parts: What theory, developed by Augustine and Aquinas, sets criteria for when warfare is morally permissible?
What Latin phrase names the set of criteria for the right to go to war, such as just cause and right authority?
What Latin phrase names the rules governing conduct within war, such as proportionality and discrimination?

q: A presbyter of Alexandria taught that the Son was created and that "there was a time when he was not." His position was condemned at a council called by Constantine in 325, which declared the Son homoousios, or of one substance, with the Father. His opponent Athanasius spent several exiles defending that ruling. For 10 points, name this heresiarch whose views were rejected at the Council of Nicaea.

This North African bishop described stealing pears as a teenager and his mother Monica's prayers in a work addressed to God. He argued that evil is a privation of good and wrote a work contrasting two cities after the sack of Rome in 410. For 10 points, name this bishop of Hippo, author of the Confessions.

This Dominican friar's five ways attempt to prove God's existence from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and design. He adapted Aristotle in a work left unfinished after a mystical experience in 1273. For 10 points, name this scholastic author of the Summa Theologica.

This German monk was summoned to an imperial assembly in 1521 and said "Here I stand." His translation of the New Testament into German helped standardize the language, and he was protected in Wartburg Castle by Frederick the Wise. For 10 points, name this author of the Ninety-five Theses who began the Protestant Reformation.

This French reformer's Institutes of the Christian Religion was first published in 1536. He led a theocratic Geneva, burned Michael Servetus, and taught that God elects some people for salvation. For 10 points, name this theologian whose followers include the Presbyterians and Huguenots.

This doctrine, associated with Calvinism, holds that God has foreordained who will be saved. It is summarized by the acronym TULIP, whose letter "U" stands for unconditional election. The Synod of Dort affirmed it against the Arminians. For 10 points, name this doctrine.

This 1545 to 1563 council met at an Italian city in the Alps and served as the Catholic answer to the Protestant Reformation. It reaffirmed seven sacraments, the authority of tradition, and the Latin Vulgate. For 10 points, name this council that launched the Counter-Reformation.

This Spanish soldier was wounded at Pamplona in 1521 and wrote the Spiritual Exercises. He founded a society approved by Pope Paul III in 1540 and was canonized in 1622. For 10 points, name this founder of the Jesuits.

This 451 council defined that Christ has two natures, divine and human, united in one person without confusion. The Tome of Leo was read at it, and it rejected Eutyches. The Oriental Orthodox churches did not accept it. For 10 points, name this ecumenical council held near Constantinople.

This Latin word, meaning "and from the Son," was added to the Nicene Creed in the West. It describes the procession of the Holy Spirit and was one of the disputes behind the Great Schism of 1054. For 10 points, give this word.

In 1054 Cardinal Humbert placed a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, leading to this break. Its main figures were Patriarch Michael Cerularius and Pope Leo IX. For 10 points, name this split between Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.

This archbishop of Constantinople denied that Mary could be called Theotokos and favored the title Christotokos. He was condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431 after being opposed by Cyril of Alexandria. For 10 points, name this namesake of a church sometimes called the Church of the East.

This British monk denied original sin and said humans could be saved by free will. He was opposed by Augustine and condemned at the Council of Carthage. For 10 points, name this theologian whose views are called a namesake heresy.

This Catholic doctrine, affirmed at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, holds that the bread and wine at Mass change in substance into the body and blood of Christ. Aquinas used Aristotelian terms to explain it. For 10 points, name this doctrine.

Lutherans teach that Christ is present in, with, and under the bread and wine, a view often called by this term. Zwingli instead argued for a purely symbolic meaning at the 1529 Marburg Colloquy. For 10 points, give this Latin-based term for the Lord's Supper, also called Communion.

This Pharisee, born in Tarsus, was struck blind on the road to Damascus after a vision. His letters to the Romans, Galatians, and Corinthians make up a large part of the New Testament. For 10 points, name this apostle to the Gentiles.

This feast, fifty days after Easter, commemorates the descent of the Holy Spirit on the apostles, who then spoke in tongues. It is sometimes called the birthday of the church. For 10 points, name this feast, also called Whitsun.

This book is often called the Apocalypse of John and was written on the island of Patmos. It describes seven seals, four horsemen, and a beast whose number is 666. For 10 points, name this final book of the New Testament.

Scholars of the Synoptic problem propose that Matthew and Luke drew on this earliest gospel and on a hypothetical sayings source called Q. It begins with the baptism of Jesus and has no birth narrative. For 10 points, name this shortest gospel.
This sermon of Jesus in Matthew 5 to 7 begins with the Beatitudes. It includes the Lord's Prayer and teaches loving enemies. For 10 points, name this sermon, delivered on a hillside.

This sixth-century Italian monk wrote a rule that divides the day into prayer, work, and reading. He founded Monte Cassino, and his motto is "pray and work." For 10 points, name this founder of Western monasticism.

This Italian saint, born Giovanni Bernardone, renounced his family's wealth and founded an order of friars. He received the stigmata and wrote the Canticle of the Sun. For 10 points, name this saint from a town in Umbria.

This English cleric founded Methodism with his brother Charles. He preached in the open air, traveled on horseback, and had a heart "strangely warmed" in Aldersgate Street in 1738. For 10 points, name this man.

This Puritan minister's sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" was delivered in Enfield, Connecticut. He was a leading figure in the First Great Awakening and later served as president of the College of New Jersey. For 10 points, name this theologian of Northampton, Massachusetts.

This Catholic council, called by Pope John XXIII in 1962, allowed the Mass to be celebrated in vernacular languages. It issued documents such as Lumen Gentium and Nostra Aetate. For 10 points, name this council in Rome.

This eighth-century and ninth-century controversy in the Byzantine Empire was about whether sacred images should be venerated. The emperor Leo III banned them, and the Second Council of Nicaea reversed the ban in 787. For 10 points, name this dispute, whose participants smashed icons.

This Swiss reformer of Zurich, a contemporary of Luther, held that the Eucharist is purely symbolic. He died fighting at the Battle of Kappel in 1531. For 10 points, name this priest who began the Reformation in Switzerland.

This Anabaptist group is named after a Frisian priest who joined in 1536. Its members practice believer's baptism, nonresistance, and plain dress. The Hutterites and Amish are related. For 10 points, name this denomination.

This Spanish Carmelite mystic wrote The Interior Castle and reformed her order with John of the Cross. A sculpture by Bernini depicts her ecstasy. For 10 points, name this woman who was named a Doctor of the Church in 1970.

In 1534 this English act of Parliament declared the king the head of the Church of England. Thomas Cranmer had already annulled the marriage of Catherine of Aragon. For 10 points, name this act, passed under Henry VIII.

This statement of faith, supposedly composed by the twelve apostles, begins "I believe in God, the Father almighty." It is recited in many liturgies and mentions the descent into hell. For 10 points, name this creed, simpler than the Nicene.
Answer these questions about early church councils.
parts: Which Roman emperor called the Council of Nicaea in 325?
Which bishop of Alexandria opposed Arius at Nicaea?
Which 431 council proclaimed Mary Theotokos, "God-bearer"?

q: Answer these questions about the Protestant Reformation.
parts: Which city in Saxony was home to the church door where Luther is said to have posted his theses?
Which Dutch humanist published a Greek New Testament in 1516 and wrote In Praise of Folly?
Which 1555 agreement allowed German princes to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for their realms?

q: Answer these questions about monastic orders.
parts: Which order of mendicant friars was founded by Francis of Assisi?
Which order, founded by Dominic in 1216, is known for preaching and the Inquisition?
Which French abbey, founded in 910, led a reform movement that gave rise to an order following Benedict's Rule?

q: Answer these questions about the New Testament.
parts: Which gospel writer was a tax collector, according to tradition?
Which book of the New Testament recounts the early church from the Ascension to Paul in Rome?
Which epistle says "the just shall live by faith" and was central to Luther's thought?

q: Answer these questions about Catholic and Orthodox practice.
parts: Which sacrament is also called Holy Communion?
Which season of forty days precedes Easter?
Which Orthodox practice of the fourteenth century, associated with Gregory Palamas, stresses the repetition of the Jesus Prayer?

q: Answer these questions about the Great Awakening and revivalism.
parts: Which Methodist founder preached in the open air to coal miners?
Which English evangelist toured the American colonies, drawing crowds in the 1740s?
Which revival preacher held a Cane Ridge meeting in Kentucky in 1801, part of the Second Great Awakening?

q: Answer these questions about Christian theologians of the twentieth century.
parts: Which Swiss theologian wrote the Church Dogmatics?
Which German pastor, executed in 1945, wrote The Cost of Discipleship?
Which American theologian wrote Moral Man and Immoral Society and the Serenity Prayer?

q: Answer these questions about Christian holidays and the liturgical year.
parts: Which season of four weeks precedes Christmas?
Which day, forty days after Easter, commemorates Christ's rising into heaven?
Which feast on January 6, called Epiphany in the West, honors the arrival of whom?

q: This text is divided into six orders, such as Zeraim and Nezikin, and was compiled around 200 CE by Judah the Prince. It records the oral law in short rulings. The Gemara later added commentary to it. For 10 points, name this first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.

Two versions of this work exist: one compiled in Babylonia around 500 CE and a shorter one from the Land of Israel. Its pages have a central text surrounded by the commentaries of Rashi and the Tosafot. It includes the Mishnah and the Gemara. For 10 points, name this central text of rabbinic Judaism.

This physician and philosopher of Cordoba and Cairo wrote the Mishneh Torah and a book that tries to reconcile Aristotle with scripture. He is known for thirteen principles of faith. For 10 points, name this author of the Guide for the Perplexed.

This eleventh-century French rabbi from Troyes wrote a clear running commentary on the Torah and the Talmud. His commentary is printed beside the Hebrew text in nearly every edition. For 10 points, name this scholar known by an acronym of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki.

The Zohar is the central work of this Jewish mystical tradition, which describes ten divine emanations called sefirot. Isaac Luria developed its idea of tzimtzum, the divine contraction. For 10 points, name this mystical tradition.

Born Israel ben Eliezer in the eighteenth century in Podolia, this healer was known as "Master of the Good Name." He taught joyful prayer and the presence of God in all things. For 10 points, name this founder of Hasidism.

The Book of Jonah is read on the afternoon of this holiday, the Day of Atonement. It ends the Ten Days of Repentance and involves a twenty-five-hour fast. The Kol Nidre prayer opens it. For 10 points, name this holiest day of the Jewish year.

This holiday, the Jewish New Year, falls on the first of Tishrei. A ram's horn called the shofar is sounded, and apples are dipped in honey. For 10 points, name this holiday that begins the High Holy Days.

This festival recalls the Exodus from Egypt and lasts seven or eight days, during which leavened bread is avoided. Families hold a seder with matzah and bitter herbs. For 10 points, name this spring holiday.

This fall festival commemorates the booths in which the Israelites lived in the wilderness. Observant Jews build a hut with a roof of branches and wave a lulav and etrog. For 10 points, name this holiday.

This holiday, celebrated on the fourteenth of Adar, recalls how a Persian queen saved her people from Haman. The scroll is read aloud, listeners use noisemakers, and people eat triangular pastries. For 10 points, name this holiday.

This winter festival lasts eight days and commemorates the rededication of the Temple after the Maccabean revolt. A candelabrum with nine branches is lit. For 10 points, name this holiday, also called the Festival of Lights.
This holiday, fifty days after Passover, celebrates the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai. The Book of Ruth is read and dairy foods are eaten. For 10 points, name this "Feast of Weeks."
This day on the ninth of Av commemorates the destruction of both Temples. Observers fast, sit on the floor, and read the Book of Lamentations. For 10 points, name this day of mourning.

This day of rest begins at sundown on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday. Candles are lit and kiddush is recited over wine, and work is forbidden. For 10 points, name this weekly day, from a Hebrew word for "rest."

These dietary laws forbid eating pork and shellfish and require separating milk and meat. They derive from Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and food may carry a hechsher certification. For 10 points, name this set of dietary rules, from the Hebrew for "fit."

This body of seventy-one sages met in Jerusalem during the Second Temple period and later in Yavneh and Tiberias. It served as a high court and legislature, and Jesus was brought before it according to the gospels. For 10 points, name this assembly.

When asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot, this first-century BCE sage said, "What is hateful to you, do not do to others." He was the head of a school opposed to that of Shammai. For 10 points, name this rabbi.

This second-century rabbi began studying at age forty and became one of the leading sages of the Mishnah. He supported the Bar Kokhba revolt and was executed by the Romans. For 10 points, name this scholar.

In 73 or 74 CE, the Zealots under Eleazar ben Yair killed themselves at this hilltop fortress built by Herod near the Dead Sea. The Roman general Flavius Silva built a ramp to take it. For 10 points, name this site.

These manuscripts found in 1947 at Qumran include the oldest known copies of the Book of Isaiah. They probably belonged to a sect often identified with the Essenes. For 10 points, name this collection, discovered by a Bedouin shepherd.

This ancient Jewish group believed in the resurrection of the dead and the oral law. Sadducees opposed them, and the Mishnah's rabbinic tradition descended from them. For 10 points, name this group, whose name may mean "separated ones."
This German Jewish philosopher, a friend of Lessing, promoted the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment. He translated the Torah into German. For 10 points, name this grandfather of a famous composer.

This Hasidic rebbe, a great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov, told allegorical stories such as the tale of the seven beggars. He taught that it is a great mitzvah to always be happy and that one should speak to God in one's own words. His followers still gather at his grave in Uman for Rosh Hashanah. For 10 points, name this founder of the Breslov movement.

This prayer begins "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one." It is recited morning and evening and is placed in a mezuzah on doorposts. For 10 points, name this central declaration of Jewish faith.

This Spanish-Portuguese philosopher was excommunicated from the Amsterdam Jewish community in 1656. His Ethics is arranged like a geometry text and equates God with nature. For 10 points, name this author of the Theological-Political Treatise.

This wall in Jerusalem is the remnant of the retaining wall of the Second Temple complex. People insert written prayers in its cracks, and it is also called the Wailing Wall. For 10 points, name this site.

This first-century historian, born Yosef ben Matityahu, wrote The Jewish War and Antiquities of the Jews. He defected to the Romans and took the family name of his patron Vespasian. For 10 points, name this author.

This code of Jewish law, compiled by Joseph Karo and published in Venice in 1565, is divided into four sections. Moses Isserles added glosses for Ashkenazi practice. For 10 points, name this "Set Table."

This German-born Jewish philosopher wrote I and Thou in 1923. He later taught at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem after leaving Germany in 1938, and he also wrote Between Man and Man. He distinguished the relationship between persons from the relationship to objects. For 10 points, name this man.
Answer these questions about the Hebrew Bible.
parts: What is the Hebrew name for the first five books of the Bible?
The Tanakh has three sections. Name the second, which contains Isaiah and Jeremiah.
Which third section of the Tanakh contains Psalms, Proverbs, and Job?

q: Answer these questions about Jewish rituals.
parts: Which ceremony marks a boy reaching religious adulthood at thirteen?
Which small leather boxes, containing scrolls, do observant Jews strap to the arm and head?
Which fringed shawl is worn during morning prayer?

q: Answer these questions about Jewish denominations.
parts: Which movement, begun in Germany in the nineteenth century, adapted worship and uses organ music and vernacular prayer?
Which movement between Reform and Orthodox was led in America by Solomon Schechter?
Which medieval group, founded by Anan ben David, rejects the oral law?

q: Answer these questions about the Second Temple and Hellenistic era.
parts: Which family led a revolt against Antiochus IV?
Which Roman general destroyed the Temple in 70 CE?
Which Jewish philosopher of Alexandria blended Plato with scripture?

q: Answer these questions about the Passover seder.
parts: What unleavened bread is eaten?
What book is read, retelling the Exodus?
Which cup of wine is traditionally set out for a prophet who is expected to announce the Messiah?

q: Answer these questions about medieval Jewish history.
parts: Which 1492 decree expelled Jews from Spain?
Which Jews, descended from Spain and Portugal, are named from the Hebrew for Spain?
Which Cordoba-born poet and philosopher wrote the Kuzari?

q: Answer these questions about the books of the Prophets and Writings.
parts: Which prophet was swallowed by a large fish?
Which prophet saw a seraph touch a burning coal to his lips, according to a call vision in the Temple?
Which book, set in the land of Uz, centers on a man who loses everything?

q: Answer these questions about modern Judaism.
parts: Which Nazi program of genocide killed six million Jews?
Which Polish-born American rabbi wrote The Sabbath and led civil rights marches with King?
Which Lithuanian-born rabbi, called the Chofetz Chaim, wrote on the laws of speech?

q: This Persian polymath born near Bukhara wrote the Canon of Medicine, which was used in European universities for centuries. His Book of Healing covers logic, physics, and metaphysics. His "floating man" thought experiment argues for the soul. For 10 points, name this philosopher, known in the West as Avicenna.

This Andalusian judge from Cordoba wrote the Incoherence of the Incoherence in reply to al-Ghazali. His commentaries on Aristotle made him known in Latin Europe as "the Commentator." For 10 points, name this philosopher, also called Ibn Rushd.

This Persian scholar left a teaching post in Baghdad after a spiritual crisis and wrote a work that attacked the philosophers on twenty points. His Revival of the Religious Sciences links law and mysticism. For 10 points, name this author of The Incoherence of the Philosophers.

This fourteenth-century scholar from Tunis wrote the Muqaddimah, an introduction to history. He discussed asabiyyah, or group solidarity, as a force that rises and declines in dynasties. For 10 points, name this historian.

This Moroccan traveler of the fourteenth century journeyed for nearly thirty years across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. He dictated an account called the Rihla and visited Mali and China. For 10 points, name this man.

This thirteenth-century poet was born in Balkh and settled in Konya after meeting the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz. His six-volume Masnavi is a major work of Persian literature. For 10 points, name this poet whose followers founded the Mevlevi order.

This Kurdish sultan of Egypt and Syria defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 and recaptured Jerusalem. He founded the Ayyubid dynasty and later made a treaty with Richard the Lionheart. For 10 points, name this ruler.

This first major battle between the Muslims and Quraysh took place in 624 near a well in the Hejaz. About three hundred Muslims defeated a force more than three times as large. For 10 points, name this battle named for the site.
